findings.message: `verbose` is collected from VERBOSE env var and printed in the config summary (with the description 'Display test results' vs 'Display summary only'), but it is never consulted anywhere in the function body. The old code had an `if (verbose)` block that called `PrintResults` for each sweep point. That entire capability was silently removed while the env var and its description were kept, giving users a false expectation that VERBOSE=1 does something.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `verbose` is read from VERBOSE env var on line 38 and printed in the config summary on line 53, but is never used anywhere else in the function. The old code had an `if (verbose)` block that called PrintResults for each sweep point. That block was removed in this rewrite while the env var plumbing was kept, so VERBOSE=1 has no actual effect.
findings.severity_justification: Users consulting the env var summary will see VERBOSE listed as a recognized option that claims to 'Display test results' — setting it will silently do nothing, which is misleading and breaks user expectations without any error or warning.
findings.category_justification: The env var description promises behavior (verbose test result output) that the code no longer implements — a discrepancy between documented/advertised behavior and actual behavior.

findings.message: The format string `"  %d  %c  %d  %c  %d  %c %4d %c %3d "` has 9 format specifiers but is passed 10 arguments (`waveOrder, sep, wordSize, sep, temporalMode, sep, blockSize, sep, unroll, sep`). The trailing `sep` has no corresponding `%c` in the format. As a result, no separator is emitted between the unroll column and the first numSubExec bandwidth column in the data row, while the header line (`" WvO %c WSz %c TpM %c BlkS %c UnR "` followed by `"%c SE %03d"`) does emit a separator before each SE column. This creates a column alignment inconsistency, most visible in CSV mode where the first bandwidth value lacks its leading comma in the format (it gets one from `"%c%7.2f"` but only because that specifier was added there to compensate).
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding correctly identifies 10 arguments for 9 format specifiers, but the claimed consequence (column alignment inconsistency) is wrong. The `%c` in `"%c%7.2f"` provides the separator before each SE value, so both header and data rows align correctly. The finding contradicts itself by acknowledging the separator comes from `%c%7.2f`. The extra `sep` argument is well-defined in C (extra args are ignored), not UB.
findings.severity_justification: Even if taken at face value, the extra trailing argument is dead code — it has no effect on output. No alignment issue actually exists.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about format string argument count and output alignment correctness.

findings.message: `ParseTransfers("1 1 " + transferStr, transfers)` unconditionally prepends "1 1 " where the first token is the number of wildcard-transfer specs to read. This hardcodes the count to 1, which means a user who sets `GFX_TRANSFER` to multiple space-separated triplets (e.g., `"G0->G0->G0 G1->G1->G1"`) will silently get only the first transfer parsed — the remainder is left unconsumed by the `iss >>` reads and quietly ignored. The PR description says the rewrite is meant to 'allow the use of multiple Transfers / wildcards', but non-wildcard multi-transfer specs do not work.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `ParseTransfers` reads `numTransfers` from the first token, which is hardcoded to 1 via `"1 1 "`. A user specifying multiple triplets in GFX_TRANSFER (e.g. `G0->G0->G0 G1->G1->G1`) gets only the first parsed and the rest silently dropped. The iss-based parser stops after consuming 1 triplet with no error or warning.
findings.severity_justification: Silent data loss — the user gets a subset of their requested transfers benchmarked with no indication that the rest were ignored. The PR description explicitly claims multi-transfer support, raising user expectations.
findings.category_justification: Logic error: the hardcoded count `1` in the prefix contradicts the claimed multi-transfer capability and causes silent truncation of user input.

findings.message: `numBytesPerTransfer` (type `size_t`) is printed with the `%lu` format specifier. On Linux x86-64 this is fine because `size_t` and `unsigned long` are both 64-bit, but the correct specifier for `size_t` is `%zu`. The old code explicitly cast to `unsigned long` (`static_cast<unsigned long>(...)`) before using `%lu`; the new code drops that cast. This is a silent portability/correctness issue for any platform where `sizeof(size_t) != sizeof(unsigned long)`.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The code at line 62 uses `%lu` with a bare `size_t` argument (confirmed), and the old code had an explicit `static_cast<unsigned long>()`. On platforms where `sizeof(size_t) != sizeof(unsigned long)` this is technically UB. The finding is factually correct, though the same pattern exists throughout the entire codebase.
findings.severity_justification: This project targets Linux/ROCm on x86-64 where `size_t == unsigned long`. In practice there's no behavioral issue on target platforms. The pattern is pervasive across the whole codebase (10+ other files), so while technically non-portable, the real-world risk is negligible.
findings.category_justification: This is a portability/code quality issue — using an imprecise format specifier — rather than a correctness bug on the actual target platform.

findings.message: If `ParseTransfers` succeeds but returns an empty `transfers` vector (possible if the wildcard expansion produces zero concrete transfers on the current topology), the validation loop is skipped (no GFX-executor check, no `t.numBytes` assignment), and the sweep proceeds to call `RunTransfers(cfg, {}, result)` repeatedly for every parameter combination. `RunTransfers` with an empty transfer list may silently succeed returning zero bandwidth, leading to a final summary claiming 'Highest bandwidth found: 0.00 GB/s' with `best = {0,0,0,0,0,0}` (default-initialized zeros). There is no guard or warning for this case.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `ParseTransfers` can return an empty transfers vector when wildcard expansion produces no matches (e.g., no GPUs on rank). The validation loop is skipped, `RunTransfers` silently succeeds returning 0.0 GB/s each iteration, and the summary reports meaningless results. The old code explicitly guarded against non-unit transfer counts.
findings.severity_justification: Produces silently misleading results (0.00 GB/s, all-zero best parameters) with no error message when the topology doesn't match the transfer spec. Users would receive a plausible-looking but completely bogus output.
findings.category_justification: Missing error handling/guard for an edge case that causes silent failure and misleading output rather than a proper error report.

findings.message: The GFX-executor type check (`t.exeDevice.exeType != EXE_GPU_GFX`) is performed inside the same loop that prints each transfer's description. If the first k transfers pass validation but transfer k+1 fails, the function has already printed partial transfer output (description lines for transfers 0..k) then returns 1 without printing the separator or any indication of which transfer caused the error. The error message itself does not include the transfer index, making it hard to diagnose in multi-transfer configurations.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: validation is inside the print loop (lines 66-80). If transfer k fails, transfers 0..k-1 have already been printed. The error message has no transfer index. These facts are correct.
findings.severity_justification: This is a diagnostic quality issue — partial output and a missing index in the error message. It doesn't cause incorrect behavior when transfers are valid, and the realistic case (wildcard expansion from a single GFX spec) would fail only if the user provides a non-GFX executor, which would typically be caught on the first transfer anyway.
findings.category_justification: The interleaved print-and-validate pattern and the missing transfer index in the error message are code quality/readability concerns affecting diagnostics, not functional correctness.

findings.message: The `BMA_EXEC_ENABLED` guard uses `HIP_VERSION` (the computed integer encoding) while all other HIP version checks in this file use `HIP_VERSION_MAJOR` directly. Modern ROCm (5.x+) encodes `HIP_VERSION` as `MAJOR*10000000 + MINOR*100000 + PATCH`, so HIP 7.1.0 = 70100000, which the new check `>= 70100000` correctly targets. However, the old code used `>= 710`, which under the new encoding is trivially true for every HIP release (HIP 1.0.0 = 10000000 >> 710), meaning BMA was unintentionally enabled on all HIP 6.x+ builds regardless of minor version. The new value is correct but the use of the computed `HIP_VERSION` constant is inconsistent with the rest of the file; using `HIP_VERSION_MAJOR > 7 || (HIP_VERSION_MAJOR == 7 && HIP_VERSION_MINOR >= 1)` would match the surrounding style.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: line 82 uses `HIP_VERSION` (computed integer) while lines 1539, 4769, and 5020 all use `HIP_VERSION_MAJOR`. The inconsistency is real. The new value 70100000 is functionally correct, but the style diverges from the established pattern in the file.
findings.severity_justification: The new check is functionally correct — it correctly gates BMA on HIP >= 7.1. The issue is purely a style/consistency concern vs. the rest of the file. No incorrect behavior results.
findings.category_justification: This is a coding convention inconsistency — using a different HIP version check style than the rest of the file — with no functional impact.

findings.message: When `RunTransfers` fails, the error message is printed and the function returns 1. However, the `Utils::Print("\n")` call at line 125 will still execute, inserting a newline into the output after the error message and before the program exits, which can be confusing. The error handling block should exit immediately or be structured to avoid this.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The `return 1` at line 121 exits the entire function, so `Utils::Print("\n")` at line 124 never executes in the error path. The finding's claim that the line 124 newline 'will still execute' after the error is factually incorrect.
findings.severity_justification: Even if the finding were correct, an extra newline in error output would be a cosmetic issue with no functional impact.
findings.category_justification: The finding makes an incorrect claim about control flow — that a statement after a `return` would still execute.

findings.message: When `bestBw` is 0.0, the `best` vector is uninitialized. This occurs if all transfer runs fail. The summary at the end will print garbage values from the `best` vector. It is better to initialize `best` with a known invalid state (e.g., -1) to make it clear that no valid combination was found, or to guard the final print statements with a check on `bestBw`.
findings.tp_fp_justification: `vector<int> best(6)` value-initializes all 6 elements to 0 — there are no garbage values. The finding's claim of 'uninitialized' is factually wrong. Additionally, if all runs fail, `return 1` inside the else block exits the function before the summary is printed, so the claimed scenario cannot reach the summary section.
findings.severity_justification: Even if the concern were valid, the worst case is printing zeros in an unusual edge case, not a crash or security issue.
findings.category_justification: The finding makes an incorrect claim about variable initialization state.

findings.message: Potential unbounded output: the nested loops print results to the console for each transfer combination, which could lead to excessive output in cases with large parameter ranges. This may overwhelm the console or logs.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is the intended behavior of a parameter sweep tool — it prints one result row per parameter combination. The output is strictly bounded by user-controlled list sizes. The finding makes no specific code claim, identifies no bug or regression, and is a generic comment that could apply to any sweep benchmark. The old code had the same loop structure.
findings.severity_justification: Even if taken at face value, 'lots of output' from a sweep tool is by design, not a defect. No actual harm is identified.
findings.category_justification: At most a vague design concern, with no specific code defect.

findings.message: Infinite loop in wildcard resolution: In `ParseRange`, if a token repeatedly fails to match any condition in the while loop, the code will not progress and cause an infinite loop. This impacts robust wildcard handling for erroneous inputs.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Lines 109-111 contain enum values, not ParseRange. The actual ParseRange at line 1159 has no infinite loop — its while loop uses strtok which always advances, and all branches unconditionally return. The finding is factually wrong about both the line numbers and the claimed infinite loop.
findings.severity_justification: The claimed defect does not exist in the code.
findings.category_justification: The finding alleges an infinite loop, which would be a reliability issue if it existed.

findings.message: Invalid error propagation strategy: the ERR_APPEND macro conflates fatal errors with warnings when populating the error list. This may lead to scenarios where minor warnings suppress subsequent, more critical validations.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The ERR_APPEND macro (at line 742, not 702-710) only returns false on ERR_FATAL — warnings are appended to the list and execution continues. The claim that warnings suppress subsequent critical validations is backwards: only fatals stop processing. The referenced line numbers are also wrong (702-710 contains GPU hardware ID macros unrelated to error handling).
findings.severity_justification: The claimed defect doesn't exist — the macro correctly handles the warning/fatal distinction.
findings.category_justification: The finding alleges incorrect error propagation, which would be a reliability concern if it existed.

findings.message: Inconsistent rank behavior: If `GetNumRanks()` at `ParseRange` receives negative or unusual values, rank parsing outputs may deviate from expectations as singular negative boundaries may bypass meaningful checks entirely.
findings.tp_fp_justification: `GetNumRanks()` is initialized to 1 and can only be negative via severe misconfiguration. `ParseRange` handles negative `fullCount` intentionally as a sentinel. Downstream validation at lines 1790-1817 catches invalid rank indices with ERR_FATAL. The finding is vague, generic, references unmodified pre-existing code, and identifies no concrete exploitable scenario.
findings.severity_justification: Even if GetNumRanks returned a negative value (requiring deliberate misconfiguration), downstream rank validation would catch invalid indices before they cause harm.
findings.category_justification: The finding alleges a potential edge case in parsing/validation that could produce unexpected behavior.

findings.message: I saw that you are manually flushing elsewhere.  Maybe it makes sense to fflush here too.  If there's a way to get the raw output stream, then using the << operator with std::endl would work.  You wouldn't have to separately call fflush.  Maybe Print should have this as an optional argument (flush/no flush).  I don't know if it matters too much one way or the other.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is explicitly non-committal ('Maybe it makes sense', 'I don't know if it matters too much one way or the other'). It proposes no concrete fix, offers several vague alternatives, and the reviewer acknowledges it may be irrelevant. This is a casual musing, not an actionable code review finding.
findings.severity_justification: Even if addressed, adding an fflush after a row-ending newline has negligible practical impact — each bandwidth value is already flushed at line 117.
findings.category_justification: At most a minor output buffering style preference with no correctness or reliability implications.

findings.message: When `ev.outputToCsv` is true, `sep` is set to `,`, but the format strings on lines 89 and 103 still hard-code multi-space padding around `%c` (e.g. `" WvO %c WSz %c ..."` and `"  %d  %c  %d  %c ..."`). The resulting CSV output therefore contains extra whitespace inside every field (e.g. `" WvO , WSz ,..."` and `"  0  ,  0  ,..."`), which spreadsheet importers will preserve as part of the cell values and which defeats the purpose of CSV mode. Consider building the format string conditionally so no surrounding spaces are emitted when `sep == ','` (or trim the columns to match the CSV use case the PR description targets).
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified in both the diff and checked-out file: format strings for the header (' WvO %c WSz %c ...') and data rows ('  %d  %c  %d  %c ...') hard-code surrounding whitespace that is emitted regardless of whether sep is ',' or ' '. When outputToCsv is true, the resulting CSV cells contain embedded spaces (e.g. ' WvO ' instead of 'WvO'), which most spreadsheet importers preserve verbatim — directly contradicting the PR's stated motivation of making output easier to import into spreadsheets.
findings.severity_justification: The broken CSV mode defeats the explicitly stated goal of the PR (spreadsheet import). Users relying on CSV output for analysis will get polluted cell values, requiring post-processing to clean up. Not a crash or data corruption, but a functional failure of a named feature.
findings.category_justification: The code does not produce the intended CSV-compatible output despite setting a sep variable for that purpose — the behavior contradicts the documented/stated intent of the CSV mode.
